# Web research

Use this skill whenever a good answer depends on information that may have changed since your training or that you are not sure of: news and recent events, prices, product versions, who currently holds a role, opening hours, schedules, rules and laws, statistics, availability. Also use it when the user asks you to look something up or research something. Don't use it for stable knowledge (definitions, history, how things work, maths, writing) unless the user asks.

## Pick the tool (strict)

Look at which tools you actually have in this reply, and pick ONE family:

1. If any chrome__ tool exists, use Chrome for EVERYTHING:

     article, then chrome__read_page.
   - Do NOT call web_fetch, web_search or any browser__ tool, even for one
     quick page, even if it seems faster. If a page won't load in Chrome,
     skip it and pick another source.
2. Else if any browser__ tool exists, use the Browser the same way, and
   do NOT call web_fetch or web_search.
3. Else if web_search / web_fetch exist, use those.
4. Else answer from what you know, with a clear warning that it may be

Before each tool call, check: "Is this tool from the family I picked?"
If not, don't call it.

## Choose the search language

Match the question: search in Danish (Google with `hl=da`, Danish words) for Danish topics, places, companies, rules or prices in Denmark, and in English for everything else. For international topics asked in Danish, search in English and answer in Danish. Answer in the language the user wrote in.

## Search: Google first, then DuckDuckGo

Write a short, specific query (3–8 words; include the year for anything time-sensitive).

**With Chrome**
- Open Google in a new tab: `chrome__tabs_create` with `https://www.google.com/search?q=<query>&hl=en` (or `hl=da`).
- Read it with `chrome__read_page`. If there is an **AI Overview** near the top, read it fully (click "Show more" if it is cut off) and note the sources it links to.
- If Google shows a robot check ("unusual traffic", captcha, "I'm not a robot"), shows a consent page you can't get past, or has nothing useful, never try to solve or get around the check. Search DuckDuckGo instead: `chrome__navigate` to `https://duckduckgo.com/?q=<query>` (or `https://html.duckduckgo.com/html/?q=<query>` if the page is hard to read). Use its "Search Assist" answer like an AI Overview when there is one.

**With the Browser**
- Use `browser__search` (it searches Google and puts the AI Overview first when there is one).
- If it reports a robot check or finds nothing useful, use `browser__navigate` to `https://duckduckgo.com/?q=<query>` and read the results.

**With Web search**
- Use `web_search` (there is no AI Overview here), then open the best results with `web_fetch`.

## Verify: the AI Overview is a starting point, not the answer

- Always open and read **at least 2 real sources** before answering: the pages the AI Overview links to, or the best search results. Prefer official and primary sources (the organisation's own site, government sites, original documentation, reputable news) over aggregators, forums and SEO pages.
- If the sources disagree, open a **third** and say plainly where they differ. Prefer the most recent and most authoritative.
- Check dates: for anything time-sensitive, use the newest information and say how recent it is.
- Never fill gaps from memory or guess URLs. If you need a page you can't find, search again with different words.
- Write down the facts you need (with their source) in your reply as you go: old tool results may be cleared in long tasks.

## Tidy up (Chrome)

- Work only in tabs you open yourself (`chrome__tabs_create` or `chrome__navigate`). Never use, change or close the user's own tabs.
- Don't sign in, fill in forms, buy, post or accept anything. If a page needs a login, skip it and find another source.
- When you're done, close every tab you opened with `chrome__tabs_close`.
- With the Browser, call `browser__close` when you're done.

## Answer

- Give the answer first, clearly and concisely, then any details or caveats (e.g. "prices vary by store", "as of March 2026").
- If you used Google's AI Overview, say so where it matters, and only state what the sources you opened confirm.
- End with a **Sources** list: one line per source you actually used, as `[Page title](URL)`, newest or most important first. Leave the list out only if the user has asked for no sources.
- If the research couldn't settle something, say what is uncertain instead of guessing.

## How deep to go

Match the effort to the question:
- Quick question ("what's the latest on X?", "who is Y?", "what does Z cost?"):
  ONE search, then read 2-3 good sources (at most 4). Then answer.
- Comparison or "explain in depth": up to 6 sources and 2 searches.
- Only go further if the user asks for thorough or deep research.
Stop as soon as 2 independent, recent sources agree on the main facts.
Don't open extra searches for side topics (stock price, lawsuits,
successors) unless the user asked about them; offer them at the end instead
("Want me to look into ...?").

Only open links you saw on a results page or inside an article. Never
type in an article address you guessed.

To open a search result or a link, click its [number] with chrome__click. Never type an address yourself unless the user gave it.

Jensen Huang has resigned as chief executive of Nvidia after reports of extramarital affairs with an alleged Chinese spy and two company employees.

He will be replaced on an interim basis by Nvidia’s chief financial officer, Colette Kress, until a full-time successor is named.

Shares in the chipmaker plunged by 13% when Wall Street opened, after Huang’s departure was announced. After a partial rebound, they closed down 4.3% on Thursday, wiping more than $180bn (£135bn) off Nvidia’s value on the day and around $490bn for the week – valuing the company at $4tn.

The statement from Nvidia’s board of directors confirming Huang’s departure did not mention the spying scandal and personal conduct revelations, instead paying tribute to Huang’s “profound” contributions to the company he co-founded.

“Jensen’s contributions to Nvidia are profound. Nvidia is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world. The board and the company thank Jensen for his immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry,” the statement said.

It added that Huang had resigned as chief executive, president and Nvidia board member “effective immediately”.

Donald Trump, who had defended Huang at first as the scandal threatened to overwhelm the Nvidia co-founder, quickly moved on to potential successors on Thursday, posting on social media that he should be replaced by Tim Cook, Apple’s former chief executive and current executive chair.

“NOW THAT Nvidia CEO JENSEN HUANG, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place – TIM COOK of Apple,” Trump wrote, adding: “A Legend replaces a Legend!”

The chipmaker’s board earlier this week [33] link "appointed the leading law firm" Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct a “thorough and independent” investigation into the relationship with Alice Huang, an Nvidia customer and Chinese citizen who is no relation to the Nvidia boss. Nvidia had previously denied anything unusual about the relationship, but that changed on Sunday when Jensen Huang admitted he had been unfaithful to his wife, Lori, without referring to Alice Huang directly.

The law firm had directed Jensen Huang to continue to lead Nvidia as the investigation continued.

However, late on Wednesday, the New York Times [34] link "reported" that Huang had a separate extramarital affair with a company employee named Kimberly Powell. She was Nvidia’s vice-president of healthcare and was reportedly captured on video being affectionate with Huang at a hotel during a company conference in March.

Nvidia’s board said it would consider internal and external candidates for the chief executive’s role, with Cook featuring among potential runners and riders before Trump’s intervention. Cook stepped down as chief executive at Apple in September but still has a senior executive role at the company. Rene Haas, the chief executive of Arm Holdings, a UK-based chipmaker, has also been mooted, along with Lisa Su, the chief executive of the chipmaker AMD.

Huang ran Nvidia tightly and managed about 60 direct reports. Internal candidates include Kress and Ian Buck, who manages the company’s AI hardware and software products. Huang’s two children, Madison and Spencer, also work at Nvidia but are in their mid-30s and relatively inexperienced. The chipmaker also announced the appointment of Harvey Jones, a tech investor and entrepreneur, as its first-ever chair.

Dan Ives, a senior US tech analyst, said the board had done what “it needed to do, which is rip off the Band-Aid and take Nvidia into its next chapter without him” and that the company remained ahead of its competitors.

However, Neil Wilson, an analyst at the investment platformSaxo UK, said Nvidia would need a “great CEO” to replace Huang.

“His technical knowledge and understanding of every last bit of product is basically unique and impossible to replicate,” Wilson said, adding nonetheless that Nvidia was well placed in terms of upcoming products and orders.

Huang’s exit from the company he co-founded in 1993 removes a senior figure in Silicon Valley at a time when the AI arms race between the US and China is at an apex. He owns more than 870m shares, or about 3.6% of the company, and was worth $145bn on Thursday morning, according to Bloomberg, making him the world’s 13th richest person.

Unlike many of his contemporaries at other leading tech companies, Huang has dozens of direct reports, an unusual management structure that emphasises his control over the company.

The entire AI ecosphere relies on Nvidia, which engineers advanced chips used to train AI models and power companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic. It is also one of the most valuable companies on Earth, with a market cap that hit $5tn at one point last year.

Huang has denied any knowledge that Alice Huang allegedly worked for the Chinese government. The pair were seen together around the world, dining in restaurants and attending meetings, over the past few years. Alice Huang is a businesswoman and head of the Singapore-based datacentre firm Megaspeed, who US intelligence services suspect of being a Chinese asset according to multiple reports.

On the same day that Jensen Huang admitted having an affair, Nvidia’s board of directors announced the company was launching an investigation regarding reports that he was the target of a foreign intelligence effort. Huang has agreed to testify before US Congress.

Nvidia makes chips used in artificial intelligence (AI) systems.

A computer chip is essentially a small piece of semiconductor material, or a set of electronic circuits. It processes information and stores data.

Nvidia is far from the only company that designs computer chips, which more broadly are used in all modern digital technology, from computers to cars to kitchen appliances. But Nvidia chips are used for many cutting-edge technologies, and are widely used in the AI industry.

The company was founded in 1993. Before the AI boom took off, it was largely known for making the type of chips that process graphics, particularly for computer games.

It has widely been considered a stock market darling in recent years, with the AI boom driving a meteoric rise in its share price.

Jensen Huang's resignation from Nvidia is not the end of the scandal, which will continue to reverberate around Washington for days, weeks and possibly months to come.

Going forward, much of the focus will be on the Trump administration's Commerce Secretary, former Cantor Fitzgerald president Howard Lutnick.

According to the New York Times, Lutnick clashed with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent over his handling of Megaspeed, the Singaporean data centre firm that was led, in part, by the woman alleged to be a Chinese spy with whom Huang reportedly had an affair.

While the commerce department has denied the clash took place, the report starkly highlights tensions within the Trump administration over its AI policy. A particular focus is technology export rules, which are overseen by the commerce department, and the over $4bn of Nvidia technology purchased by Megaspeed.

Even before today's resignation, House Democrats had publicly demanded that Lutnick be called to answer questions about the administration's AI and export control policies, which they have claimed endanger US national security.

It has also been reported by Axios was sent a highly classified memo regarding Huang's affair and the alleged connection to Chinese intelligence.

Lutnick has so far not commented on the issue, and Trump has suggested only that Apple's Tim Cook take the reins of Nvidia.
